title: Instructional coaching: how to help prison officers to keep getting better at the job November 12, 2026
author: Unlocked Graduates
summary: Unlocked Graduates argues that prison officers rarely get to rehearse the skills they perform daily, so poor habits harden on high-pressure wings and spread through inexperienced staff. The proposed remedy is instructional coaching: codify the relational and procedural skills of the job into teachable techniques, model them, and have officers practise deliberately with supportive feedback. The piece lists four obstacles (performance plateau, the forgetting curve, lack of personalisation, habit formation under pressure) and six elements of a working model, including culture, resources, group training, observation, feedback and tracking. Leaders are urged to be observed too, so that development rather than judgement defines the culture. The authors report better practice quality, more metacognition and greater enjoyment of the role. The central claim is that leaders improve a workforce by making improvement small, specific and regular.
points: Officers perform almost constantly and rehearse almost never, which lets ingrained, less effective habits form and spread across whole wings.
Coaching begins by codifying good practice into concrete techniques, supported by a pocket guide, poster, slides and model videos usable in real time.
The cycle is identify, set a goal, break it down, see a model, practise, get feedback, and repeat until the skill is habitual.
Coaching must serve development and not judgement, and leaders should model it by being observed themselves.
Reported results include better relational practice, more staff metacognition and greater enjoyment of the role.
quotes: Prison wings are also high cognitive load environments, which means habitual actions and reactions form fast and become very hard to change.
Prison officers spend almost all their time performing in real situations, with very little chance to rehearse.
This turns intangible skills into concrete, teachable behaviours, so officers develop consistently, and just agreeing what good looks like prompts useful conversations about professional practice.
Leaders should model these behaviours so continuous improvement becomes part of everyday work.
Instructional coaching works because it makes improvement small, specific and regular, and because it brings rehearsal, which prison work rarely allows, into the job itself.
Use instructional coaching for development, not judgement. Share feedback openly and celebrate progress, aiming for steady improvement.
